newsitem.title: GERMANY: Freed German envoys describe Peru siege ordeal.
newsitem.headline: Freed German envoys describe Peru siege ordeal.

text.p: Two high-ranking German diplomats released from the besieged Japanese embassy residence in Peru said in German television interviews on Monday their captors had treated them well but conditions were deplorable.
Juergen Steinkrueger, deputy ambassador to Peru, said in an interview with RTL television a lack of food, water and electricity made the situation very difficult.
"It feels good to be free. These were hard days for all of us," Steinkrueger told RTL, according to an advance transcript of a programme to be broadcast on Monday evening.
"The hostage-takers treated us well, although we were a large group of people in a small space. The entire episode was very unpleasant because the provisions were very bad.
"I am happy to be with my family for Christmas, but it hasn't yet ended for the rest of the hostages," he added.
Germany's ambassador to Peru, Heribert Woeckel, described in another RTL interview how the conditions in the residence had deteriorated. Woeckel was released last week.

"In the first night there were about 400 people in a small house. We were sitting or lying down in any corner we could find. I wasn't able to close my eyes for the whole night. The television was on the whole time. The hostage-takers were watching everything very carefully.
"The next day none of us had enough sleep, we were not able to wash, there were only two toilets. We had to stand in line."
Woeckel said the Marxist rebels at first had appeared "nervous", but gradually began to calm down.
"It was horrible," he said. "The hostage-takers were raving mad and nervous in the beginning. We had to throw ourselves on the ground, the local police shot tear gas at us."
Woeckel said the hostages were then separated according to nationalities.

"We were then allowed to make phone calls. I called the German embassy. At first we were only allowed to talk in Spanish, the kidnappers listened carefully to everything we said. Then they let us talk in our own languages to our governments and families."
